title: Angular momentum conservation implies rotational kinetic energy conservation
statement: When a system conserves angular momentum under zero external torque, its rotational kinetic energy must also remain conserved.
incorrect_statement: When a system conserves angular momentum under zero external torque, its rotational kinetic energy must also remain conserved.
erroneous_reasoning: Students treat mechanical energy conservation and angular momentum conservation as interdependent or coextensive laws. They assume that if an isolated system has zero net external torque, mechanical kinetic energy must automatically be conserved, neglecting the internal non-conservative work performed when mass is redistributed radially within the rotating body.
why_it_fails: Rotational kinetic energy is K_rot = L^2 / (2 I). When mass moves radially, moment of inertia I changes while L remains constant, so K_rot scales inversely with I. Internal muscular forces or sliding friction do work, causing mechanical kinetic energy to change dramatically despite perfect conservation of angular momentum.
correct_physics_explanation: Conservation of angular momentum requires only that the net external torque about the axis of rotation is zero: $\tau_{\text{ext}} = 0 \implies L = I \omega = \text{constant}$. In contrast, mechanical kinetic energy conservation requires that the net work done by all non-conservative forces (both external AND internal) is zero: $W_{\text{nc, ext}} + W_{\text{nc, int}} = 0$. Rotational kinetic energy can be expressed directly in terms of angular momentum as $K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \frac{L^2}{2I}$. If the mass distribution of the system reconfigures internally (such as a figure skater pulling in their limbs, an insect crawling outward on a turntable, or two rotating discs clutching via friction), the moment of inertia changes from $I_1$ to $I_2$. Because $L$ is constant, $K_{\text{rot}} \propto \frac{1}{I}$. If $I$ decreases, $K_{\text{rot}}$ increases (the extra energy is supplied by positive internal muscular work done against centrifugal forces). If $I$ increases, $K_{\text{rot}}$ decreases (energy is dissipated or absorbed by internal non-conservative work). Thus, conservation of angular momentum does NOT imply conservation of kinetic energy.
corrective_explanation: Conservation of angular momentum requires only that the net external torque about the axis of rotation is zero: $\tau_{\text{ext}} = 0 \implies L = I \omega = \text{constant}$. In contrast, mechanical kinetic energy conservation requires that the net work done by all non-conservative forces (both external AND internal) is zero: $W_{\text{nc, ext}} + W_{\text{nc, int}} = 0$. Rotational kinetic energy can be expressed directly in terms of angular momentum as $K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \frac{L^2}{2I}$. If the mass distribution of the system reconfigures internally (such as a figure skater pulling in their limbs, an insect crawling outward on a turntable, or two rotating discs clutching via friction), the moment of inertia changes from $I_1$ to $I_2$. Because $L$ is constant, $K_{\text{rot}} \propto \frac{1}{I}$. refutation_counterexample: A figure skater of moment of inertia $I_1 = 4.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ spins freely with angular velocity $\omega_1 = 5\text{ rad/s}$ ($L = 20\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$, $K_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2 = 50\text{ J}$). By pulling in their arms, the skater halves their moment of inertia to $I_2 = 2.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$. Under zero external torque, $L$ is conserved, so $\omega_2 = L / I_2 = 20 / 2.0 = 10\text{ rad/s}$. The new kinetic energy is $K_2 = \frac{1}{2} I_2 \omega_2^2 = \frac{1}{2} (2.0) (10)^2 = 100\text{ J} = 2 K_1$. Rotational kinetic energy has doubled (+50 J of biological muscular work), proving conclusively that angular momentum conservation does not imply kinetic energy conservation.
supporting_evidence: H.C. Verma, Concepts of Physics Vol 1, Section 10.18: 'Conservation of Angular Momentum'; I.E. Irodov, Problems in General Physics, Problem 1.258; Questions rotational-motion-question-84f91c20 and rotational-motion-question-f7cbecda.
diagnostic_symptom: Student sets initial KE equal to final KE in problems involving changing rotational inertia (e.g., student solving for final angular velocity by writing (1/2) I1 w1^2 = (1/2) I2 w2^2).
